findings.title: Misleading comment about what the code does
findings.body: The comment says "check upstream availability" but the code checks `response.ok`, which tests whether the HTTP response status was 200–299. A server is "available" even when it returns a 500 error — `response.ok` would be false, but the upstream is reachable. Conversely, if the upstream is truly unavailable (DNS failure, connection refused), `fetch` throws before reaching the `ok` check. The comment should say something like "check HTTP response status" or be removed as unnecessary.

findings.body: The old `pending` map ensured that two simultaneous `loadCached(k, fn)` calls would only invoke `fn()` once, sharing the resulting promise. The new code calls `fn()` for every concurrent caller. If `fetchValue` is expensive or has side effects, this is a correctness and performance regression. Restore a `pending`-like map, or use an async mutex pattern to guard the fetch.

findings.title: Concurrent request deduplication removed, fetchValue can run multiple times for the same key
findings.body: The original code used a `pending` map so that concurrent calls with the same key shared one in-flight promise; the second caller would await the same promise instead of calling `fetchValue` again.  The new code removes that guard — if two calls arrive before the first `fetchValue` resolves, both enter the `if` body, both call `fetchValue`, and the second result silently overwrites the first.  This wastes work (e.g. duplicate API calls) and means callers can see different values for the same key depending on timing.  Either restore the `pending` map pattern or introduce an equivalent in-flight tracker.

In modern Node.js this will crash the process via `unhandledRejection`; in browsers it produces a console warning. The promise must be awaited or have a `.catch()` handler.

Either await the response and return its status, or at minimum add a `.catch()` to handle failures. findings.title: Inverted access control check after refactor

The original checked `!canEdit(...)` to reject unauthorized users; now `assertEditable` checks `canEdit(...)` and throws when the user IS authorized. This means authorized edits are rejected with 'cannot edit', while unauthorized edits silently succeed. Fix: restore the negation to `if (!canEdit(doc, userId))`.

findings.title: Validation narrowed from all-falsy to undefined-only, missing empty string and null
findings.body: The original `if (!id)` caught empty string, null, and undefined. The replacement `if (id === undefined)` only catches undefined. An empty string `""` or explicit `null` will pass through and produce `{ id: "" }` or `{ id: null }`, which downstream code almost certainly does not handle correctly. The function signature says `id: string` but runtime values like `null` or `""` are not ruled out. Either restore the broad falsy check or add explicit validation for all invalid inputs.

findings.title: Failure mode changed from throwing to silent null return without callers expecting it
findings.body: The original threw an Error, which forced callers to handle the invalid-id case explicitly. The replacement silently returns `null`, which shifts a programming error into a possible `Cannot read properties of null` crash at the call site (or worse, a silent data corruption if the null is propagated). This is a breaking behavioral change that should be accompanied by an updated return type (`loadUser(id: string): { id: string } | null`) and updated callers, or the throw should be retained.

findings.title: Validation narrowed from all falsy ids to only undefined
findings.body: The original `if (!id)` guarded against empty string, null, and undefined. The new check only catches `undefined`. Since `id` is typed `string`, `undefined` is unlikely in well-typed callers, meaning the most realistic bad input—empty string—now silently produces a user object with `id: ""`. The comment on line 2 (`// dogfood: missing validation on empty id`) confirms the author is aware of the gap. Restore a check that rejects empty strings, e.g. `if (!id)`, or add an explicit `id.trim().length === 0` guard.

If the intent is to degrade gracefully, consider returning `null` for all invalid inputs (empty string included), not just `undefined`.

findings.title: Unbounded retry loop removes all backstop
findings.body: Changing `while (attempts < 3)` to `while (true)` removes the maximum‑attempt guard. If `job.run()` never succeeds, this loop will run forever, consuming CPU and potentially causing resource exhaustion or denial of service. Restore a capped bound (e.g. `while (attempts < 3)` or a configurable max).

findings.title: Unbounded retry loop with no termination condition
findings.body: The loop was changed from `while (attempts < 3)` to `while (true)`, removing the only exit path for repeated failures. If `job.run()` throws consistently, this retries forever — no limit, no backoff, no circuit breaker. This will exhaust resources (CPU, I/O, connections) and hang the caller. Add a maximum attempt count and either break after exhausting it or throw from the catch block when the limit is reached.

findings.title: Dead code after infinite loop — throw is unreachable
findings.body: The `while (true)` loop on line 10 can only exit via the `return` on line 13 (success). If the job keeps failing, the loop iterates forever, so control never reaches line 19. The throw statement and its error message are dead code that will never execute. Either reintroduce a loop guard so the throw becomes reachable, or move the throw into the catch block when the limit is exceeded.
